 Joint task force on haze mulled
 Thursday, 29 Oct 2026

Air supply: A mobile oxygen bus being deployed by the Palangka Raya local government in Central Kalimantan to help residents struggling with severe haze pollution. — Reuters 
 JAKARTA and Singapore are looking to set up a joint task force to deal with haze from Indonesia’s wildfires, the countries’ foreign ministers said, as they met to reaffirm their ties after weeks of simmering tensions.
 The visit to Jakarta by Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan came amid mounting frustrations in the city-state over the transboundary haze generated by Indonesia’s most intense forest fires in 11 years.
 After a two-hour meeting on Tuesday, Singapore and Indonesia’s top diplomats discussed establishing a task force that would enable the countries to share information, gather cross-border evidence and potentially even recover assets from companies linked to the forest fires, Indonesia’s Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said.
 “We must follow the money trail these companies have left behind.
 “Singapore offered to share data on companies linked to the fires,” Nasir said.
 “No border should shield those who profit from burning our forests.”
 Indonesia has previously launched criminal investigations into companies linked to the fires.
 Nasir added that the two countries were mature enough to talk candidly about the fires, which have caused a spike in respiratory illnesses in Indonesia and engulfed neighbouring Singapore, Malaysia and Timor Leste in smoke.
 “Singapore stands in solidarity with Indonesia. (Haze) is a common problem, and one that we can best achieve collectively,” Balakrishnan said after the meeting.
 Both foreign ministers said the first victims of the haze were Indonesians, with Balakrishnan vowing to crack down on companies registered in Singapore found to be responsible for the fires.
 In their remarks, neither minister mentioned the tensions arising from Jakarta’s decision to cut gas supplies to the city-state.
 Jakarta cut pipelined gas to Singapore by about 8% as of Saturday, saying it was safeguarding domestic supplies.
 Singapore ​generates up to 95% of its electricity from natural gas, and though the supply cut from Indonesia amounts to less ​than 2% of daily demand, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Sunday that he expects contract signatories to “honour their commitments”.
 Indonesia’s energy minister, Bahlil Lahadalia, hit back on Monday, saying the amount of gas now being supplied to Singapore met the minimum level stipulated under their agreement.
 “Our nation is a nation that honours contracts, rules. So don’t lecture Indonesia on how to honour contracts,” Bahlil said.
 Veteran Singaporean diplomat Bilahari Kausikan called the gas cuts an “attempt at intimidation” but said they would be ineffectual.
 Singapore’s state investor Temasek and its sovereign ‌wealth fund GIC were also on the defensive last week, rejecting allegations by a former Indonesian trade minister that they had pressured global index provider MSCI to consider demoting Indonesia’s equities to “standalone” market status. — Reuters
